title: z-index & Stacking Contexts
summary: **z-index** controls the front-to-back stacking order of overlapping elements — but only inside a **stacking context**. Understanding how contexts form (via position, opacity, transform, and more) is the key to fixing 'my z-index: 9999 isn't working' bugs.

subtopics.title: Painting order without z-index
subtopics.explanation: When nothing sets z-index, the browser paints in a defined order: background and borders first, then non-positioned blocks, then floats, then inline content, then positioned elements in source order. So a later positioned element naturally sits on top of an earlier one. z-index only enters the picture to override this default.
subtopics.example: /* Later in the DOM paints on top by default */

subtopics.title: z-index only works on positioned (or flex/grid) items
subtopics.explanation: z-index has no effect on a statically positioned element (the default). It applies to elements with position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky — and to flex and grid items even when statically positioned. This is the single most common reason z-index 'does nothing': the element isn't a stacking participant.

subtopics.title: What a stacking context is
subtopics.explanation: A stacking context is a self-contained group of elements that stack together as a unit. z-index values only compete WITHIN the same stacking context. An element with z-index: 1 inside one context can never appear above an element in a sibling context that stacks higher — no matter how large its z-index.
subtopics.example: /* z-index is relative to the parent context, not the page */

subtopics.title: What creates a stacking context
subtopics.explanation: Many things create a new stacking context: a positioned element with a z-index other than auto; opacity less than 1; any transform, filter, perspective, clip-path, or mask; will-change of a context-triggering property; isolation: isolate; position: fixed/sticky; and flex/grid children with a z-index. Each new context traps its children's z-index.

subtopics.title: z-index trapping (the classic bug)
subtopics.explanation: When a parent creates a stacking context, its children's z-index values become local to that context. A child with z-index: 9999 can still appear behind a sibling of the PARENT that has a higher z-index, because the child is trapped inside the parent's stack level. The fix is usually to raise the parent or restructure the DOM.
subtopics.example: /* child z-index: 9999 still trapped under parent's level */

subtopics.title: isolation: isolate
subtopics.explanation: isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context without needing position or z-index, and without side effects like opacity changes. It's a clean, intentional way to scope z-index for a component so its internal layering can't leak out or be affected by outside z-index values.

foundations.overview: When elements overlap, something has to decide which one is in front. The browser has a default painting order, and z-index lets you override it. The catch is that z-index doesn't operate on a single global scale — it operates inside stacking contexts, which form for many reasons beyond z-index itself. Most z-index confusion comes from not seeing the invisible stacking contexts in play.
foundations.formalDefinition: z-index is a CSS property that sets the stack level of a positioned (or flex/grid) element within its stacking context; higher values paint in front of lower ones among siblings in the same context. A stacking context is an isolated 3D layering scope in which child stack levels are resolved.
foundations.whyItMatters: Modals, dropdowns, tooltips, sticky headers, and overlays all depend on correct stacking. Getting it wrong leads to elements hidden behind others or 'z-index wars' of ever-larger numbers that don't help.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of stacking contexts as a tree of transparent sheets. Each context is one sheet; z-index orders elements drawn on that sheet. A child's z-index can never lift it above a sheet that sits in front of its own sheet — you can only reorder within the sheet you're on.
foundations.browserPerspective: During painting, the browser walks the stacking-context tree. For each context it paints negative-z-index children, then the background/non-positioned content, then positioned children by ascending z-index. Properties like opacity and transform force the element onto its own composited layer and create a new context, which is why they affect stacking.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Layering modals above page content, keeping tooltips above dropdowns, pinning sticky headers above scrolling content, and scoping a component's internal layers with isolation so they don't fight global z-index.
foundations.businessImpact: Reliable layering keeps critical UI — cookie banners, modals, CTAs — visible and clickable, directly protecting conversions and accessibility.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing what creates a stacking context turns z-index from guesswork into a deterministic system, eliminating brittle '9999' hacks and regressions when adding transforms or opacity.
foundations.performanceImpact: Context-triggering properties (transform, opacity, will-change, filter) often promote elements to their own GPU layer; this can improve animation smoothness but, overused, increases memory and compositing cost.
commonUseCases: Ensuring a modal overlay sits above all page content
Keeping tooltips and dropdowns above their triggers
Pinning a sticky header above scrolling body content
Scoping a component's layering with isolation: isolate

commonMisconceptions.myth: z-index is a global scale; a bigger number always wins.
commonMisconceptions.reality: z-index only compares siblings within the same stacking context; a child can't escape its parent's stack level.
It only affects positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky) and flex/grid items; on static elements it does nothing.
opacity < 1, any transform/filter/clip-path, will-change, isolation, and fixed/sticky positioning all create new stacking contexts.

steps.title: Default painting
steps.description: With no z-index, elements paint in source order; later positioned elements naturally sit on top.

steps.title: z-index needs positioning
steps.description: z-index only takes effect on positioned (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky) or flex/grid items.

steps.title: A context forms
steps.description: A parent with opacity: 0.9 (or a transform) creates a new stacking context, isolating its children.

steps.title: The child gets trapped
steps.description: The child's z-index: 9999 now only competes inside the parent's context, not against the whole page.

steps.title: Resolving it
steps.description: Raise the parent's stack level, remove the context trigger, or use isolation deliberately to scope layering.

interactiveExamples.title: Basic stacking with z-index
interactiveExamples.explanation: Two positioned, overlapping boxes; z-index decides which sits in front within the same context.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Red box B overlaps and sits in front of blue box A because of its higher z-index.

interactiveExamples.title: z-index trapped by a parent context
interactiveExamples.explanation: The parent's opacity creates a stacking context, so the child's huge z-index can't escape past the sibling.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The red sibling covers the blue child even though the child has z-index 9999, because opacity trapped the child in the parent's context.

debuggingLab.title: My z-index: 9999 dropdown is hidden behind a card
debuggingLab.symptom: A dropdown with z-index: 9999 still renders behind a neighboring card with a small z-index.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: transform: translateZ(0) on .toolbar creates a new stacking context, trapping the dropdown's z-index: 9999 inside it. The toolbar itself has no z-index (auto), so it stacks at the same level as the card — and the card's z-index: 5 wins. The dropdown's huge value never competes with the card directly.
commonMistakes: Adding a transform/opacity/will-change to a parent without realizing it creates a stacking context.
Escalating the child's z-index instead of fixing the parent's stack level.
Assuming z-index is global rather than per-context.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Remove the context trigger on the parent (or give the toolbar a z-index above the card) so the dropdown can stack over it.

theory.question: What is z-index and when does it actually take effect?
theory.directAnswer: z-index sets the front-to-back stack order of overlapping elements. It only takes effect on positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) and on flex/grid items — it has no effect on statically positioned elements. Higher values paint in front, but only among siblings in the same stacking context.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A property that assigns a stack level within an element's stacking context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To override the browser's default source-order painting when elements overlap.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Within a stacking context, the browser paints children by ascending z-index; z-index values from different contexts never compare directly.

theory.whyImportant: Almost every overlay UI depends on it, and 'why doesn't my z-index work' is a staple intermediate interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: A modal overlay uses position: fixed with z-index: 100 to sit above the page content.

nestedTopics.title: Requires positioning
nestedTopics.explanation: z-index does nothing on static elements (except flex/grid items).

nestedTopics.title: Per-context comparison
nestedTopics.explanation: z-index only orders siblings in the same stacking context.

nestedTopics.title: Default painting
nestedTopics.explanation: Without z-index, later positioned elements paint on top.

followUps.question: Does z-index work on flex or grid children without positioning?
followUps.answer: Yes — flex and grid items respect z-index even when statically positioned.

followUps.question: Can a negative z-index be useful?
followUps.answer: Yes, a negative z-index can place a positioned element behind its parent's background content within the same context.

theory.question: What is a stacking context and what creates one?
theory.directAnswer: A stacking context is an isolated layering scope in which child z-index values are resolved independently from the rest of the page. Many things create one: a positioned element with z-index other than auto, opacity < 1, any transform/filter/perspective/clip-path/mask, will-change of those properties, isolation: isolate, and position: fixed or sticky. Once a context forms, its children's z-index can't escape its stack level.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A self-contained group of elements that stack together as one unit relative to outside elements.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To allow predictable, composable layering and to support GPU compositing for properties like opacity and transform.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser builds a tree of stacking contexts; z-index orders elements within a context, while the context's own level orders it among its siblings.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding context creation is what separates deterministic layering from endless z-index escalation, and it's a strong senior-level signal.
theory.realWorldExample: Adding opacity: 0.99 to a card to fade it unexpectedly traps a tooltip inside it, hiding the tooltip behind later content.

nestedTopics.title: Triggers
nestedTopics.explanation: opacity, transform, filter, will-change, isolation, fixed/sticky, and positioned + z-index all create contexts.

nestedTopics.title: Trapping
nestedTopics.explanation: Children's z-index is local to the context; it can't lift them above the context's own level.

nestedTopics.title: isolation: isolate
nestedTopics.explanation: Creates a context intentionally with no other side effects.

followUps.question: How do you debug an unexpected stacking context?
followUps.answer: Inspect ancestors for opacity, transform, filter, or will-change in DevTools; any of these creates a context that can trap z-index.

scenario.question: A tooltip inside an animated card (with a transform) renders behind the next card. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The transform on the card creates a stacking context, so the tooltip's z-index is trapped inside that card and can't rise above the sibling card. Fix it by raising the card's own stack level when active (or removing the transform), or by rendering the tooltip in a portal at the body level so it lives outside the trapped context.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A z-index trapping problem caused by a transform-created stacking context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: transform forces the element onto its own composited layer and forms a stacking context, localizing descendant z-index.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Either elevate the parent context, drop the trigger, or move the overlay out of the context via a portal.

scenario.whyImportant: Tooltip/dropdown clipping by transformed ancestors is one of the most common real-world layering bugs.

nestedTopics.title: Transform = context
nestedTopics.explanation: Any transform creates a stacking context, trapping descendants.

nestedTopics.title: Portals
nestedTopics.explanation: Rendering the overlay at the body root sidesteps ancestor contexts.

followUps.question: Why do component libraries render dropdowns in portals?
followUps.answer: To escape ancestor stacking contexts and overflow clipping, so the overlay layers and positions against the viewport instead.

coding.question: Write CSS for a full-screen modal overlay that sits above all page content, with the dialog above the backdrop.
coding.thoughtProcess: The overlay must cover the viewport and stack above the page, so use position: fixed with inset: 0 and a high z-index. To layer the dialog above the backdrop cleanly, scope the overlay as its own stacking context (the high z-index does that) and let the dialog stack inside it.
coding.lineByLine: position: fixed + inset: 0 makes the overlay cover the viewport. z-index: 1000 lifts it above page content and creates a stacking context. The flex centering positions the dialog. .dialog is positioned with z-index: 1 so it stacks above the backdrop inside the overlay's context.

alternativeApproaches.title: Native <dialog>
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The <dialog> element with showModal() handles top-layer stacking above all content automatically, bypassing z-index entirely.

followUps.question: How does the native <dialog> top layer differ from z-index?
followUps.answer: showModal() promotes the dialog to the browser's top layer, which always paints above normal stacking contexts regardless of z-index values.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Manage z-index with a small, named scale (e.g. tokens: dropdown 1000, sticky 1100, modal 1300, toast 1500) rather than ad-hoc numbers. Scope component internals with isolation: isolate so a component's layers never leak into the global scale, and render overlays (modals, tooltips) via portals to escape ancestor stacking contexts.
productionDeepDive.performance: Context-triggering properties (transform, opacity, filter, will-change) promote elements to GPU layers, which helps animation but costs memory if overused. Apply will-change sparingly and only around active animations.
productionDeepDive.security: Stacking has no direct security surface, but invisible or mis-layered overlays can enable clickjacking; ensure interactive overlays are actually on top and that hidden elements aren't accidentally receiving clicks.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Centralize z-index tokens so teams don't escalate into z-index wars. Document which components own which layers and reserve ranges for system UI like modals and toasts.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Comment any opacity/transform that exists for visuals but also creates a stacking context, so future edits don't cause mysterious layering regressions. Prefer isolation: isolate when you intentionally want a context.
productionDeepDive.observability: Chrome DevTools' Layers panel and the 'create stacking context' annotation in the Elements pane reveal hidden contexts; the 3D view helps visualize the stack tree.

caseStudies.problem: Tooltips and dropdowns were clipped or hidden by transformed/opacity ancestors.
caseStudies.solution: Portal-based overlays plus a centralized z-index token scale and isolation for component internals.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Portals complicate event bubbling and positioning logic.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat z-index as a system, not per-element numbers, and escape contexts deliberately.

keyTakeaways: z-index only affects positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky) and flex/grid items — not static elements.
z-index values only compete within the same stacking context; a child can't escape its parent's stack level.
Many properties create a stacking context: positioned + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, isolation, and fixed/sticky.
The classic bug is z-index trapping: a parent's opacity/transform localizes a child's huge z-index. Fix the parent, not the child.
Use isolation: isolate to scope a component's layering, a z-index token scale to avoid wars, and portals to escape ancestor contexts.
